title: Coordinator, Digital Health (Ethiopia)
description: This role was posted on August 13, 2026. Please note that we will review applications on a rolling basis. About Last Mile Health Last Mile Health saves lives in the world's most remote communities. Our vision is a health worker within reach of everyone, everywhere. We partner with governments to recruit, train, equip, and integrate professional community health workers into national health systems, equipping them to deliver quality primary care in rural and remote communities. Founded in Liberia in 2007, we now operate programs in Ethiopia, Liberia, Sierra Leone, and Malawi. Our global offices are located in Accra, Ghana and in the United States. We are looking for mission-driven leaders to join us as we work to ensure no patient is out of reach. About The Ethiopia Team The Ethiopia team works in partnership with Ethiopia’s Ministry of Health to strengthen the country’s flagship Health Extension Program, a globally recognized model for delivering primary healthcare through more than 40,000 Health Extension Workers. Led by Abraham Zerihun, the team works to upskill the Health Extension Workers through blended learning that combines digital and in-person training. It also advances digital innovation through HEP Assist, an AI-powered clinical decision-support tool that helps Health Extension Workers provide evidence-based care at the point of service. The team's portfolio spans maternal, newborn, child health, nutrition, and non-communicable diseases, including hypertension, diabetes, eye care, and stroke prevention and management, while strengthening health systems through sustainable community health financing, resource mapping, and strategic planning to support long-term government leadership and program sustainability. The Role At Last Mile Health (LMH), we make bold commitments that inspire innovation. Do you have experience supporting digital health implementation, troubleshooting technology in the field, and working with frontline health workers to deploy and strengthen digital health solutions? If so, you may be the next Digital Health Coordinator at Last Mile Health. The Digital Health Coordinators will provide high level technical and implementation support for the deployment of LMH's digital health tools to Community Health Workers (CHWs) across Ethiopia, including Extension Essentials and HEP Assist AI. Reporting to the Director, Digital Health, Ethiopia, the Coordinators will support planning, coordination, and implementation of digital health activities, working closely with program teams, field teams, and users to ensure effective adoption and use of digital health solutions. Based in Addis Ababa, the role will provide hands-on support to digital health implementation and will travel to different regions as needed to support field deployment and training activities. The Coordinators will support workplan management, data collection and feedback processes, data analysis and dashboard development, application installation and troubleshooting, and the development and implementation of processes and procedures that strengthen digital health activities. The role will also provide remote technical support to users through phone, email, and relevant open source digital health communities. This advertisement is for two Digital Health Coordinator positions based in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia. This is a fixed-term position for 24–36 months, with the potential for renewal. The role is based onsite in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, and is open only to candidates who are currently located in and authorized to work in Ethiopia. What You'll Do Digital Health Solutions Implementation Coordination Coordinate with the Senior Digital Health Coordinators to ensure that the digital health initiatives are run successfully across all districts Work with the Director, Digital Health, Senior Manager of Digital Health, Ethiopia country office program team, the Global DH Manager, and other relevant internal LMH departments (MERL, HSS, etc.) to maintain and update deployment tasks in the implementation plan Roll out new Deployment Packages (latest apps and tools such as Extension Essentials and HEP Assist AI) to Health Extension Workers (HEWs) Support establishment of a digital health management processes and procedures for digital health activities Support Digital Health Training activities including the planning and deployment of a digital education platform for Health Extension Workers Coordinate, facilitate and participate in health worker and health systems leaders trainings across districts Support learners (health workers, Ministry of Health (MOH) and health system leaders) during training (including app installation on mobile device, etc.) and remotely after training Support LMH and MOH program managers/ Coordinators in creating user accounts for app access and maintain dashboards to track learners sync status and course performance Support data collection efforts for all digital health activities including data tracking, data

title: Consultant - Final Evaluation Coherence programme Ethiopia
description:
1. Introduction The COHERENCE programme Ethiopia 2022-2026 is implemented by Ethiopian Catholic Church – Social and Development Commission Soddo branch (ECC-SDCO/S) and Adigrat branch (ECC-SDCO/Ad) , with coordination support by the East Africa regional programme Manager CI.be. The programme is implemented in 7 countries and is co-funded by the Belgian Government. The program’s aim is to equip rural communities so that they become more resilient and can better cope with crisis situations. Above all, the program wants the most vulnerable people, particularly women, young people and people with disabilities, to have expanded opportunities to improve their living conditions. Through a ‘triple nexus ’ approach, focus is on (1) social cohesion, peace-building and rights protection within communities; (2) rural economic development; and (3) disaster preparedness The present terms of reference relate exclusively to the final evaluation of COHERENCE Ethiopia. The final evaluations of the three other country programs are the subject of separate tenders and fall outside the scope of this assignment. 2. Object of the evaluation: COHERENCE Ethiopia 2.1 Program objective, results and activities To address food insecurity of poor and vulnerable households – with a focus on female-headed and landless households – of 2 kebeles in Damot Woyde district (Wolaita) and 2 kebeles in Irob district (Eastern Tigray) , COHERENCE Ethiopia aimed to improve their livelihood base in a sustainable way, by means of a triple nexus approach, linking three complementary areas: social cohesion, rural economic development and disaster risk reduction (DRR). The action’s specific objective was formulated as follows: “By the end of 2026, poor and vulnerable households, especially resource poor female-headed and landless households, in two kebeles (Endamosa and Hareze Sabata) of Irob district and two kebeles (Kindo Koyo and Mayo Kote) of Damot Woyde district have strengthened their livelihood basis, better enabling them to seize opportunities and realize their aspirations”. The objective was to be achieved through three results. A first result concerned social cohesion that was to be improved by building household and community capacity to manage resource-induced conflicts and to ensure equitable and fair access or entitlement to natural resources, through, among others: Conducting a rapid gender context analysis at community level (1 in each intervention area); Organizing in groups and training of 180 community cohesion and gender empowerment agents on peace building, conflict management and facilitation skills; Organizing community dialogue sessions on peace and conflict management and gender equity (while applying the household transformation method); Rehabilitating and expanding water piping to address existing water access conflict (Wolaita); Planting tree seedlings on communal land between communities as a joint, social cohesion enhancing activity (Tigray); Providing energy-saving stoves for 300 households (Wolaita). The direct causes of food insecurity in the intervention zones are – besides the two-year war in Tigray (2020-2022) – the depletion of household assets and continuous dwindling of income. Repeated food shortages have also forced many households to sell their assets to address immediate needs. Therefore, through a second result , the program aimed to contribute to improving household production, income, savings and productive assets by: Supporting households in income generating activities and household asset building; Organizing, training and equipping savings and and internal lending groups (SILCs) to enhance solidarity, savings and resilience; Selecting specific Household Asset Building Packages (HABP), providing technical and basic business training of HABP-SILC groups, and supporting households in financing business plans by means of subsidy. Finally, a third result sought to strengthen vulnerable households' resilience in response to climate-induced shocks and stress, by focusing on improving farm production by: Organizing volunteer smallholders in “community learning groups” (type of farmer field schools) and providing orientation training on Resilience Design (RD); Facilitating self-assessments based on local knowledge, practices and exchange; Increasing soil fertility with appropriate durable techniques identified using a RD approach; Supplying farm-resilient seeds and biological catalysator (for compost making) (Tigray); Providing energy-saving tools for households with special needs; Conducting quality monitoring and group learning of RD-related activities implemented at farm-level through community learning groups or famer field school groups. In addition, by means of workshops, exchange visits, networking and inclusive and participatory MEAL, stakeholders were expected to mutually reinforce each other's capacities, in particular with regard to issues addressed by the program. 2.2 Target groups COHERENCE Ethiopia’s implementation period extended over 42 and 36 months respectively in Wolaita and Eastern Tigray, addressing a total of at least 1,900 households (1,000 in Wolaita and 900 in Eastern Tigray). More specifically, the program targeted: With regard to social cohesion: 1,900 households (1,000 in Wolaita, 900 in Tigray) of which 1,327 are male-headed (787 in Wolaita, 540 in Tigray) and 573 female-headed (213 in Wolaita, 360 in Tigray), 4 peace and social cohesion and gender equity promoting groups, and 180 peace and social cohesion agents / community leaders (elders, religious leaders, women and youth representatives, …) (75 in Wolaita, 105 in Tigray); With regard to rural economic development (household asset building): 830 poor households (400 in Wolaita, 430 in Tigray) with priority for female-headed and landless households, and 49 SILCs (20 in Wolaita, 29 in Tigray); With regard to disaster risk reduction (resilience design): 800 smallholder households (600 in Wolaita, 200 in Tigray), with a priority for smallholders vulnerable to climate change; Government technical staff. In addition to these target-groups, i.e. direct beneficiaries, the following indirect beneficiaries were foreseen: The population of the 2 kebeles (Endamosa and Hareze Sabata) in Eastern Tigray and of the 2 kebeles (Kindo Koyo and Mayo Kote) in Wolaita; Government services and local authorities of the 4 kebeles; Authorities of Irob and Damot Woyde districts. 2.3 Three innovative approaches Three approaches are assumed to have particularly contributed to the action’s achievements and are to receive specific attention during the final evaluation (see evaluation questions below). 2.3.1 Social cohesion and peace building through village peace agents To encourage peace building and social cohesion, COHERENCE Ethiopia mobilized volunteers from the targeted communities who were expected to become “change agents”.They were trained on basic peace building and conflict management and thus equipped with knowledge and skills on grassroots conflict prevention, management and resolution. Thereto, the program adopted the so-called the 3Bs/4Ds methodology (cf. https://ics.crs.org/resource/ties-bind-building-social-cohesion-divided-communities ) that combines binding, bonding and bridging (the 3Bs) with appreciative inquiry (the 4Ds: discover, dream, design and deliver) to enable communities to cooperate and collaborate across ethnic, religious, gender, class and other divides and to strengthen horizontal and vertical rights relations and social cohesion. Following this methodology, key grassroots actors were accompanied in discovering their individual and collective strengths and their mutual responsibilities in promoting social cohesion. At the heart of the methodology is a focus on what connects and energizes people, rather than on obstacles and issues that separate them. The trained change agents were to facilitate “community dialogues sessions” that focused on tensions and conflicts that had been identified through a rapid conflict analysis and a limited social cohesion barometer survey. 2.3.2 Gender empowerment Apart from promoting peace and social cohesion, the community volunteers were also expected to be change agents with regard to gender relations in their community. They were trained on gender analysis and participatory gender transformative methods and tools. A rapid gender context analysis was conducted and based on its findings, gender transformation activities were engaged in by the program at two levels. First, at village level, trained change agents organized, in collaboration with the program’s community animators, community conversation sessions on gender issues with groups of men and women, giving participants room to talk, discuss and exchange ideas about gender perceptions and roles in their households and at community level. Next, using two complementary gender transformation methods (the Household Transformation Method (HTM) and Gender Action Learning (GAL) ), male and female members of households were supported in assessing and analyzing intra-household gender disparities (division of labor, access to and control of household resources, benefits sharing mechanisms, decision-making power, etc.). Ultimately, the approach was to result in bringing about change and improvement in terms of the gender empowerment index. 2.3.3 Community Learning Groups Co-creation and sharing of knowledge plays a central role in the process of developing and implementing agroecological innovations including climate change adaptation. To create together and share knowledge, farmers need a platform that supports them to work in small groups and have opportunities to articulate ideas, increase their motivation and participation to innovate and adapt, build trust and collaborate among themselves and with other stakeholders (e.g. extension workers) and strengthen effective linkages with stakeholders. One way in which co-creation and knowledge sharing can be encouraged is by establishing and strengthening Community Learning Groups (CLG) at grassroots. While in other approaches Farmer Field Schools (FFS) or Farmer Training Centers (FTC) are used as centers where people go and learn or acquire knowledge, a CLG is a group of active and interested individual farmers organized for peer-to-peer learning and experience or knowledge sharing, regardless of age, sex and social group. Most of the time, experience sharing and visiting events take place among members and external experts and trainers are invited on demand only. Farmers participating in the Ethiopia program thus established such CLGs. While participating in these groups, they implemented resilience design activities concerning soil health, soil and water conservation and crop diversification. Group membership is based on proximity of farmland. The program strengthened the CLGs’ capacity by means of an orientation session and training on the CLG approach and its objectives and its added value compared with other extension approaches. With the support of the program, the CLGs established bylaws and appointed their leadership (chairperson, secretary and record keeper). They meet once per month to share experiences and to learn. For each meeting the agenda – including issues for discussion, whether or not to invite external persons, etc. – is set by the CLG leaders in consultation with members. The CLG members visit each other’s farm, possibly accompanied by a development agent (DA), to see and exchange on and learn from the resilience design activities that were accomplished at the farm. The CLG approach was expected to encourage dissemination of good practices within and outside communities. Within a community, larger CLGs could be divided into smaller ones at village-level or below, so that the number of people participating in experience exchange could be multiplied. The budget of COHERENCE Ethiopia is 849,799 Euro. 3. Purpose and objectives of the evaluation The final evaluation of the COHERENCE Ethiopia program aims at: Identifying lessons learned in the introduction and adoption of social methodological innovation in view of future programming by CI.be and its partners; Ensuring accountability towards donors and other stakeholders , by rendering public the results of program performance assessment. These two objectives will be accomplished by answering three evaluation questions concerning the implementation of the three methodological approaches – presented above in § 2.3. – within the overall HDP nexus perspective. These approaches – respectively involving village peace agents, gender transformation and community learning groups – are considered innovative and key to the achievement of the program’s outcome. The intended users of the final evaluation’s results include the following: Implementation and coordination teams of partners ECC-SDCO/Ad and ECC-SDCO/S; CI.be staff at regional offices and head office and partner staff involved in joint development programming; Staff of other development actors (through publication of the final evaluation report on the CI.be website); DGD, the program donor (accountability). 4. Scope of the evaluation, evaluation criteria and evaluation questions With regard to its scope, the final evaluation will cover the COHERENCE Ethiopia program in both intervention areas, that is, in both Wolaita and Eastern Tigray, although – given the uncertain security situation in Tigray – fieldwork is expected to be restricted to solely Wolaita. Focus will be on the performance of three innovative methodological approaches, implemented by the program within a nexus approach: village peace agents, gender transformation and community learning groups. The DAC criteria that will be taken into account include coherence , effectiveness and sustainability . In addition, particular attention will be paid to the performance of the intervention in terms of inclusiveness in the fight against poverty and organisational strengthening of the target groups. The following evaluation questions are proposed (to be refined and prioritised during the framing phase): To what extent was the nexus approach adopted by the program appropriate and adequate foraddressing the target groups’ priority needs? [DAC criteria: coherence and sustainability] To what extent were the pathways of change and assumptions (theory of change) and the intervention logic (results framework) coherent, plausible and feasible? To what extent were the three innovative approaches (village peace agents, gender transformation and community learning groups) critical in the adopted design of the nexus approach? To what extent did they contribute to integrating the three pillars of the nexus (synergies between the pillars)? To what extent did the innovations fall short in reaching the different vulnerable groups targeted by the program (LNOB)? What have been the roles and contributions of the three innovative approaches (village peace agents, gender transformation and community learning groups) in achieving program outcomes ? [DAC criteria: effectiveness and sustainability] To what extent and how have the three innovative approaches beeneffective in bringing about behavioral change and adoption of new practices at target group level? Which are the factors that were conducive to these changes ? Which factors can be identified that have hindered or slowed down changes? To what extent did the 3 methods function better than other existing alternative methods in achieving program outcomes? To what extent and how are the three innovative approaches transformative? Can we see early signs of enduring changes in norms and systems ? To what extent has the program created enabling mechanisms to sustain the positive effects induced by the three innovative approaches?[DAC criteria: coherence and sustainability] How appropriate was the process of introducing the three innovative approaches within the targeted communities? Did the program learn from and adapt these innovative approaches or other activities during their implementation? What was the contribution of the MEAL process in this? To what extent do the stakeholders of the intervention – including government actiors and target groups – take ownership of the results achieved by means of the three innovative approaches and how committed are they to sustaining these results after the program’s closure? To what extent has the program built capacities of key stakeholders (implementing partners, government sector offices and target groups) required to institutionalize the innovative approaches without forsaking grassroots ownership and leadership and allowing continued flow of benefits? For each evaluation question clear and relevant lessons on introducing innovations are to be identified for use in the formulation and implementation of future programs and projects, in terms of: Operationalizing the nexus; Achieving program outputs and outcomes; Sustaining outcomes and institutionalizing approaches. 5. Approach and methodology The evaluator's offer in response to this tender should include, as part of the technical offer, a methodological proposal that shows how the evaluator will proceed to achieve the evaluation’s objectives, to make the evaluation useful and to present results that meet high quality standards. The evaluator will favour participatory methods wherever possible. The teams in Ethiopia suggest a combination of a theory-based approach (using comparative case studies) and outcome harvesting. The methodological proposal will contain : A preliminary evaluability assessment , which should demonstrate the main conditions and limitations that the evaluation will face in achieving the planned objectives and in finding answers to the questions posed. It will also indicate how evaluability problems can be solved; The general theoretical-methodological approach that will guide the final evaluation ; A proposal for accompanying the documentation process (case studies) that the project teams will engage in themselves in complement to the final evaluation and for integrating that documentation in the approach and conduct of the final evaluation itself; A proposal for an analytical framework/evaluation matrix for the external evaluation, including evaluation questions, evaluation criteria, means, and sources of information. This matrix is a tool for the implementation of the evaluation questions, but does not replace the theoretical-methodological approach that will guide the evaluation and that should be presented in a clear and differentiated way in the proposal; A description of the evaluation techniques and tools that will be used to collect, classify, analyse and present the required data . The use and analysis of existing and accessible quantitative data is expected. The use of quantitative methods requiring the collection of primary data by the evaluator is not requested. The following sources of information will be made available to the evaluator (list not exhaustive): The theory of change and the program proposal including the results framework; Baseline survey report; Internal narrative annual reports, performance scores and lessons learned (2023-2025, and draft documents for 2026); Monitoring data collected and reports produced by the implementing partners; Resource persons at the level of CI.be and implementing partners. Other documents can be provided upon the evaluator’s request (e.g. concerning meetings, trainings, etc., organised within the framework of the program). 6. Coordination of the evaluation The final evaluation will be coordinated by CI.be’s regional program manager based in Addis Ababa and Ethiopia desk in Brussels, with the support of CI.be’s MEAL officer. The regional program manager and desk officer will be first points of contact of the evaluator, with whom meetings will take place at least at certain specific moments of the process: initial briefing, finalisation of the terms of reference and framing note, discussion of the detailed methodological approach, etc. The regional program manager and desk officer will be responsible for monitoring, accompanying and facilitating the final evaluation process, and more concretely for: Facilitating the evaluator’s access to relevant sources of information (documentation, data, people); Facilitating communication between the evaluator, program implementation teams and partners, and other stakeholders; Monitoring and quality assurance of the process. The formulation of these terms of reference relied on an ongoing consultative process with the implementing partners ECC-SDCO/S and ECC-SDCO/Ad throughout the program. They will also be consulted during the final evaluation at appropriate times (framing note, draft evaluation report, etc.). Logistics of the evaluation will be coordinated by the regional program manager and ECC-SDCO/S and ECC-SDCO/Ad. 7. Reports and feedback Nature of the documents to be delivered According to a timetable agreed at the start of the evaluation and in accordance with § 8.2, the evaluator will provide the following documents and reports: A methodological “framing note” specifying the approach and methods that will be used by the evaluator to collect the required data and information; A provisional evaluation report presented for discussion and comment to CI.be and the implementing partners; A final evaluation report taking into account the remarks made on the provisional report and/or adding in annex the collection of comments not taken into account, accompanied by the reasons for not doing so. Quality of the documents Reports should be understandable and easy to read. The results and analyses must be detailed. Causal links between findings, conclusions and recommendations should be clearly visible and sequences of reasoning clearly expressed. Conclusions and recommendations should be well argued and usable in an optimal way by the final evaluation’s stakeholders (CI.be and partners, DGD, other stakeholders, ...). It is therefore important that the recommendations are limited in number number and presented in order of priority and that they are operational in order to facilitate CI.be’s and partners’ management responses. Where relevant, different options available can be explored as well as risks and limitations associated with each option. Structure of the final report Table of contents ; List of abbreviations and acronyms; Executive summary (maximum 1 page, including main findings and recommendations, with interpretation); Key information on the program and the methodology used; Well-argued findings on the evaluation questions and DAC criteria (analysing the collected and accessed data); Conclusions and recommendations, including a synthetic table presenting findings – recommendations – targeted actor (maximum 4 pages); Annexes: Terms of Reference; implemented work program (activities, list of people and organizations met, …); list of documentation consulted; inventory and documentation of lessons learned; comments not taken into account, with reasons for not taking them into account. Even though the inventory and documentation of lessons learned is presented in an annex, it should be treated as of equal importance to the main report. 8. Practical aspects 8.1 The process Phase 1: framing the assignment The evaluator will finalise the methodological approach proposed in their offer on the basis of initial briefings by CI.be and a first reading of the documents (as mentioned in § 5) shared with them. The documentation will be made available to the evaluator at the start of their work. This stage will be an opportunity for the evaluator and CI.be and its partners to conclude possible refining of the evaluation questions presented in § 4. Phase 2: documentation through case studies The partners and implementation teams in Eastern Tigray and Wolaita can engage in case studies, intended to complement the documentation process and to support the external evaluation. CI.be encourages that such case studies are organized, while being accompanied methodologically by the evaluator, who then monitors and validates the process and its relevance for the final evaluation. Phase 3: desk study and preparation of field visit During this phase, the main stakeholders involved in the field visit will be identified. The evaluator will interview online or in-person key staff of CI.be at head office and regional office, read the available documentation and develop a methodological approach (including a timetable, persons and/or groups to be met and organisation of first local feedback meeting/workshop). Phase 4: field visit The fieldwork will concern only the action in Wolaita, given the uncertain security situation in Eastern Tigray. Primary data collection will take into account budget constraints as well as the existence of particular implementation problems, etc. It will focus on those locations and key persons that are considered most relevant in assessing the three methodological innovations in the nexus approach. Sufficient time needs to be planned for methodological briefing and participatory analysis involving the implementation team and stakeholders in Wolaita. The field visit should enable triangulation of the information obtained from the reading and analysis of the documentation of the action with primary data and participatory analysis and sense making with the program teams of the two partner organizations and CI.be’s regional program manager. To allow the Eastern Tigray project team’s involvement in this sense making, they will be invited to participate in the feedback workshop to be organized in Wolaita (to the extent that the budget allows). Phase 5 : data analysis, reporting, presentation and feedback The evaluator will analyse the collected data and produce a draft report, to be presented and discussed at an online feedback session, in which CI.be, ECC-SDCO/S and ECC-SDCO/Ad will participate. Taking into account these discussions, the evaluator will finalise the evaluation report. S/he will be free to take the comments into consideration or not. However, the remarks which s/he does not take into account must be included in an annex, together with the justification for not taking them into account. In addition, the evaluator is expected to present and participate in an online sensemaking meeting with the program teams of all 7 country programs. The evaluation plan calls for findings and relevant actions to be shared and analysed among country program teams in order to be appropriately leveraged and ensure a collective, horizontal learning process. 8.2 Available budget COHERENCE Ethiopia has foreseen a budget of € 15,000 for its final evaluation, which the offer should not exceed. The amount is understood to be exclusive of expenses related to mobilization of target groups, fieldwork logistics, etc. Otherwise, the tender must include all costs associated with carrying out the assignment: fees, travel expenses, daily allowances, insurance, reproduction costs and any other expenses. The financial offer is deemed to be firm and final. The successful contractor must include in their tender a detailed work plan setting out the number of days worked per activity and per member of the evaluation team, as well as indicative dates and locations. This work plan will be discussed and approved as part of the methodological framing note. The payment terms are as follows: 30 per cent on signing the contract, 40 per cent upon submission of the draft report, and 30 per cent upon approval of the final report. 8.3 Calendar Indicative calendar: Tender: 09/2026 Analysis of offers: 09/2026 Decision on contract: 10/2026 Briefing: 10/2026 Methodological framing note: 10/2026 Documentation process by partners: 10/2026 - 11/2026 Desk study: 10/2026 - 11/2026 Field visit :11/2026 - 12/2026 Draft reporting and feedback: 12/2026 - 01/2027 Final report: 01/2027 Management response: 01/2027 Sharing of report: 02/2027 Multi-country sense making meeting: 12/2026 - 01/2027 8.4 Profile of the evaluator The evaluation should preferably be carried out by a mixed team of consultants. CI.be encourages gender balance among applicants. Required expertise and experience: Program design, implementation, monitoring and evaluation, including outcome harvesting; Organisation of participatory evaluations; Capacity building of grassroots institutions and empowerment; Technical expertise areas: HDP nexus and conflict-sensitive development; Gender equity and empowerment; Agroecology; Social cohesion and peacebuilding (small p); Rural development and social technology innovation; Proficiency in "results-based management" and "theory of change" methods; Geographical experience in Ethiopia and knowledge of the local context (Wolaita, Eastern Tigray); Knowledge of local languages. The CVs of the evaluator and their team proposed for this evaluation must be attached to the technical and financial offer. 8.5 Selection of the evaluator Tenders will be evaluated on the basis of the quality of the technical offer (80%) and the price of the services offered (20%). The technical offer will be evaluated on the basis of: The methodological approach and understanding of the terms of reference; The proposed approach to the practical organisation of the evaluation (indicative timetable of the different phases); The qualifications and experience in the different fields mentioned above of the expert and team members proposed for the evaluation. For the technical offer, the tenderer must obtain 60% of the points relating to this criterion. If not, the bid will be disregarded. The financial offer (20%) will be evaluated on the basis of: The overall package price (10%); the score (NPX) for the price of offer X will be calculated as follows: NPX = 10 x (lowest bid price)/(bid price X); The average price for a day's service (10%); the score (NPMX) for the average price for a day's service of offer X will be calculated as follows: NPMX = 10 x (lowest average price)/(average price of offer X). The average price per day of service will be calculated by dividing the sum of salary/per diem/accommodation for the evaluation team by the number of days of service offered. All bidders commit to not having any conflict of interest in relation to the program to be evaluated, including in its preparatory phases. 9. Transparency, confidentiality, ethical standards and data ownership 9.1 Transparency and confidentiality The reports to be published will not contain any information that could endanger partners, teams or any other stakeholder, compromise the integrity of the program in any way, or pose any other risk in terms of confidentiality, particularly with regard to the European Union’s General Data Protection Regulation. The evaluator is required to respect the confidential nature of all documents and data to which they have access during the evaluation process. The results of the evaluation are intended to be made public, in the interest of accountability to the donor and external stakeholders. 9.2 Ethics The evaluator carries out their work in accordance with the quality standards and ethical principles customary in the evaluation sector, including independence of judgement, impartiality, transparency of methods, reporting of findings to those concerned, and respect for the dignity of the people interviewed. The free and informed consent of interviewees is obtained prior to any interview or focus group discussion. Participants are informed of the purpose of the evaluation, how their comments will be used, and their right to refuse answering or to withdraw at any time. Comments reported in the final report are anonymised, unless the persons concerned have given their explicit written consent. Particular attention is paid to the protection of vulnerable individuals. The evaluation team shall immediately report to CI.be any situation brought to its attention that could constitute a breach of personal integrity. 9.3 Conflict of interest Candidates shall declare, in their tender, that there is no conflict of interest, whether actual or apparent, with CI.be, ECC-SDCO/S and ECC-SDCO/Ad or the donor. In particular, a conflict of interest is deemed to exist where a person has designed, implemented or evaluated all or part of the intervention that is the subject of this evaluation, or where they have a contractual, financial or personal relationship that could compromise the independence of their judgement. Any conflict of interest arising in the course of the assignment must be reported without delay. The concealment of a conflict of interest constitutes grounds for termination of the contract. 9.4 Ownership and retention of data All data collected, transcripts, recordings, field notes, databases and deliverables produced in the course of the assignment are the exclusive property of Caritas International. The evaluator may not publish, disseminate or reuse all or part of these materials for any other purpose, nor transfer them to third parties, without prior written authorisation of the commissioning bodies. Personal data shall be processed in accordance with the General Data Protection Regulation, stored securely for the duration of the assignment and destroyed, or handed over to the commissioning parties, no later than 1 month after the final report has been approved. A certificate of destruction shall be provided.

How to Apply: Interested candidates are invited to submit a technical proposal and a financial proposal. Proposals must not exceed 10 pages, excluding any attached CVs. The **technical proposal** shall include: • A methodological proposal; • A detailed work plan; • The CVs of the proposed team members, together with a breakdown of roles and responsibilities; • Professional references and an example of a relevant previous evaluation work; • A sworn statement confirming the absence of any conflict of interest. The **financial proposal**, quoted in euros, shall be broken down by type of cost and by man-day. It is to be a firm quote, inclusive of tax, and shall include all costs relating to the service. Offers must be sent by 30 September 2026 to Dorry Hagos (d.hagos@caritasint.be), with copies to Mark Breusers (m.breusers@caritasint.be) and Jozef Serneels (j.serneels@caritasint.be). If you have any questions or requests for information regarding this call for offers, please contact d.hagos@caritasint.be and/or m.breusers@caritasint.be.

(ex: Berlin or Bensheim (Germany), UK (Cambridge or remote), the US (remote), Nairobi (Kenya), Abuja (Nigeria), Lomé (Togo), Yaoundé (Cameroon), Lusaka (Zambia), Addis Abeba (Ethiopia), Guatemala City, Kampala (Uganda), Niamey (Niger), etc.). Professional proficiency in both English and French. Willingness to travel internationally and work flexibly across time zones. Identification with the Christian values and mandate of CBM. Terms of Reference for IUCN Consultancy Title: Provision of Vehicle Rental Services Objective of the Consultancy This consultancy has the following objective: 1. To secure reliable transportation services for staff coordinating and supporting the implementation of the NbS4Water Africa – Ethiopia Awash Project Background Project Reference: - Donor reference: DN01983 About IUCN IUCN is a membership Union uniquely composed of both government and civil society organisations. It provides public, private and non-governmental organisations with the knowledge and tools that enable human progress, economic development and nature conservation to take place together. Created in 1948, IUCN is now the world’s largest and most diverse environmental network, harnessing the knowledge, resources and reach of more than 1,400 Member organisations and around 15,000 experts. It is a leading provider of conservation data, assessments and analysis. Its broad membership enables IUCN to fill the role of incubator and trusted repository of best practices, tools and international standards. IUCN provides a neutral space in which diverse stakeholders including governments, NGOs, scientists, businesses, local communities, indigenous peoples organisations and others can work together to forge and implement solutions to environmental challenges and achieve sustainable development. Working with many partners and supporters, IUCN implements a large and diverse portfolio of conservation projects worldwide. Combining the latest science with the traditional knowledge of local communities, these projects work to reverse habitat loss, restore ecosystems and improve people’s well-being. www.iucn.org https://twitter.com/IUCN/ About the Project The project focuses on promoting catchment protection through Nature-based Solutions (NbS), framed as best adaptive practices in the context of climate change and increasing land degradation. It aims to scale up NbS for watershed restoration in alignment with national basin development, land degradation neutrality, and landscape restoration goals. The general objective is to enhance water-related ecosystem services in key watersheds of the Awash sub-basin for the benefit of both people and the environment through the application of NbS. To achieve this, the project will strengthen action-oriented partnerships among community-based organizations (CBOs), the wider public, national and local governments, and non-government actors. These partnerships will promote NbS that build knowledge, shape positive attitudes, and encourage good practices, mobilizing society as a whole to achieve large-scale watershed rehabilitation, restoration, and sustainable development and use. The general objective of the project is to improve ground water recharge of the little Akaki catchment of the upper Awash river basin focusing on Guleel & Addis Ketema sub-cities of Addis Ababa and Sululta town of Sheger city, specifically in Bilisuma micro catchment. Description of the Assignment The overall objective of this procurement is to competitively select and contract qualified vehicle rental or leasing service provider(s) capable of providing reliable, safe, well-maintained, and appropriately insured vehicles to support the implementation of the NbS4Water Africa – Ethiopia Awash Project. The selected service provider(s) will provide vehicles based on the operational requirements of IUCN. Scope of Work The selected service provider shall provide vehicle rental and/or lease services to IUCN in accordance with the agreed requirements and on a call-off basis, as and when required. The services may include, but are not limited to, the following: Vehicle Provision The selected service provider shall provide safe, reliable, well-maintained, and roadworthy vehicles that meet IUCN’s operational and field-activity requirements. Vehicles shall be suitable for both urban and off-road travel and shall comply with all applicable Ethiopian legal, safety, registration, insurance, and roadworthiness requirements. Vehicle Condition and Standards The primary vehicle category required under this procurement is: Toyota Hilux Double Cab 4x4 – 2.8L Diesel, model year 2020 or newer. Vehicles offered shall be in good mechanical and physical condition, regularly serviced and maintained, and equipped with all standard safety features and legally required documentation. IUCN reserves the right to inspect and approve vehicles prior to deployment and to reject any vehicle that does not meet the agreed specifications or required safety and operational standards. 2. Drivers Where vehicles are provided with drivers, the service provider shall ensure that drivers: Have updated CVs and hold valid and appropriate driving licenses. Have relevant experience and familiarity with Ethiopian road and traffic conditions. Demonstrate safe and professional driving practices. Comply with IUCN security and safety requirements. Maintain professional conduct when interacting with IUCN staff, partners, consultants, and other passengers. 3. Geographic Coverage and terms of service To establish high operational predictability and commercial confidence for the selected Vendor, IUCN defines the service framework under the following mandatory terms: Contract Duration : The baseline framework agreement shall remain valid for a fixed period of Six (6) months , subject to satisfactory performance and potential project timeline extensions. Service Frequency : Vehicle deployment will operate on an occasional, "as-needed" project basis rather than continuous, uninterrupted daily operations over the 6-month period. Minimum Utilization Guarantee : To secure the Vendor’s revenue stability, IUCN guarantees a minimum billing and deployment commitment of four (4) operational days per week for any week in which the vehicle service is activated or called up. Rate Cap Consistency for Additional Days : If project demands require the vehicle to be utilized beyond the 4-day minimum in a given week (up to 7 days), the Vendor agrees to maintain the exact same pro-rated daily rate established for the baseline minimum contract days. No premium, overtime surcharge, or inflated short-term rates shall apply for these additional active days. 4. Responsibilities of the Service Provider and Work Norms The selected service provider shall: Provide suitable vehicles according to agreed specifications. Ensure all vehicles are properly maintained and roadworthy. Ensure that all required legal documentation and insurance remain valid throughout the contract period. Provide qualified drivers where required. Ensure timely replacement of vehicles in case of mechanical failure or other operational issues. Respond promptly to IUCN transport requirements. Maintain appropriate communication with the designated IUCN focal person. Ensure compliance with applicable health, safety, security, environmental, and legal requirements. Provide accurate invoices and supporting documentation for services provided. Immediately inform IUCN of any incidents, accidents, delays, or issues affecting the delivery of services. Duration of the Assignment The duration of the vehicle rental/lease agreement will be Six- months . The contract may include an option for extension subject to satisfactory performance, availability of funding, and IUCN procurement procedures. Deliverables and Activities The consultant will provide the following deliverables and carry out the following activities: Deliverable/Activity - Description - Timeline Contract Signing and Mobilization - Signing of the contract and confirmation of vehicle availability - November 10th 2026 Vehicle Deployment - Deployment of vehicles according to IUCN requirements - November 15th 2026 Provision of Transport Services - Continuous provision of vehicle rental/lease services as requested - Throughout contract period Maintenance and Replacement - Regular maintenance and timely replacement of vehicles when required - Throughout contract period and at-least on a quarterly basis Service Reporting and Invoicing - Submission of service records and invoices - Monthly Contract Completion - Completion of services and final reporting - April 2027 Payment Schedule The Timetable below summarises the chronological order of deliverables and indicates milestones at which IUCN will pay the Consultant. Deliverable - Payment Arrangement Vehicle rental/lease services- Payment based on agreed rates and actual services provided Monthly service provision - Subject to submission and approval of invoice and supporting documentation Additional approved services, if any - Payment based on agreed rates and prior approval by IUCN Skills and Experience The consultant must have the following skills, education and experience as a minimum: Valid business registration and trade license authorizing vehicle rental, leasing, transport, or related services. Relevant experience in providing vehicle rental or leasing services. Availability of a suitable fleet of vehicles. title: Consultancy - Addressing the Intersection of Climate, Conflict and Gender Equality in the Turkana-Omo Borderlands (Project Number: 2878-03/2023)
description:
International Alert (Kenya and Horn of Africa) in partnership with Turkana Pastoralists Development Organization (TUPADO) and the Ethiopian Institute of Peace in Ethiopia (EIP) is implementing the project “ Addressing the intersection of climate, conflict and gender equality in the Turkana-Omo borderlands.” The project funded by the Austrian Development Agency (ADA) began implementation in August 2024 and will end in March 2027. The project seeks to strengthen gender-inclusive local institutions and governance mechanisms capable of effectively managing transboundary conflicts linked to climate risks. It does this through a combination of community engagement, institutional strengthening, women's leadership promotion, cross-border dialogue, and policy influencing. These integrated approaches are designed to strengthen trust, foster collaboration across borders, enhance local ownership of conflict management processes, and support evidence-based policy influence at county, national, and regional levels. Context and Background General Background In the Horn of Africa, protracted conflicts over natural resources, especially water and pasture in the dryland borderlands are exacerbated by climate shocks disproportionately affecting the politically and economically marginalised pastoralist communities. The Turkana-Omo transboundary area between northwestern Kenya (Turkana County) and southern Ethiopia (South Omo zone) are characterized by recurrent drought and floods, weak governance systems, and deep-seated gender inequalities which drive escalating resource-based tensions among the Turkana, Dassanech and Nyangatom communities. Declining fish stocks, combined with rising lake levels that displace landing sites and communities intensify competition for water and fisheries. Cross-border cattle raiding has become increasingly commercialised and violent, and authorities are often unable to halt attacks or recover stolen livestock. These overlapping pressures erode livelihoods, food security and social cohesion in the borderlands. Conflict and climate impacts are deeply gendered. Women face heightened vulnerability during raids and displacement, bear the burden of rebuilding homesteads, and turn to diverse income generating activities after livestock losses. Harmful masculinities link cattle raiding to rites of passage, manhood and bride price obligations. Despite their frontline roles, women are systematically excluded from male-dominated peacebuilding and climate adaptation mechanisms. The project operates in two transboundary corridors linking these communities, seeking to address the interconnected drivers of conflict, climate vulnerability and gender inequality. Background to the Project International Alert in partnership with Turkana Pastoralists Development Organization (TUPADO) and the Ethiopian Institute of Peace in Ethiopia (EIP) is implementing the project “Addressing the intersection of climate, conflict and gender equality in the Turkana-Omo borderlands.” The project funded by the Austrian Development Agency (ADA) began implementation in August 2024 and will end in March 2027. The project seeks to strengthen gender-inclusive local institutions and governance mechanisms capable of effectively managing transboundary conflicts linked to climate risks. It does this through a combination of community engagement, institutional strengthening, women's leadership promotion, cross-border dialogue, and policy influencing. These integrated approaches are designed to strengthen trust, foster collaboration across borders, enhance local ownership of conflict management processes, and support evidence-based policy influence at county, national, and regional levels. The overall goal of the intervention is to reduce conflicts exacerbated by climate change and climatic shocks in the borderlands of the Horn of Africa through gender-responsive peacebuilding. The intended outcome is “Strengthened gender-inclusive formal and non-formal structures and actions to effectively manage transboundary conflict linked to climate risks affecting communities in the Omo-Turkana border area of Kenya and Ethiopia” To achieve this outcome, the intervention is structured around four output areas: • Output 1 – Women, youth and other vulnerable groups are empowered to meaningfully participate in cross-border conflict management and climate adaptation formal and informal institutions • Output 2 – Well coordinated Communities and local institutions structures established and capacities to manage conflict issues driven by climate change enhanced • Output 3 – Local governance actors (formal and informal) empowered and coordinated to manage transboundary conflict and climatic shocks in a gender sensitive way • Output 4 – Policymakers at the national and regional level (including government, multilaterals, and civil society) are integrating learning on the intersection of conflict, gender equality and climate action into policies and programmes. Implementation is guided by several cross-cutting themes, namely gender equality and women’s empowerment, youth inclusion, conflict sensitivity, climate adaptation and resilience, social inclusion, and cross-border cooperation. Evaluation Purpose and Objectives Purpose of the Final Evaluation The purpose of this Final Evaluation is to provide an independent and evidence-based assessment of the project’s achievements and contribution to strengthening climate-resilient and gender-responsive peacebuilding systems in the Kenya-Ethiopia borderlands. The evaluation will support accountability to stakeholders and document challenges and lessons learned during implementation. It will provide practical recommendations to inform future programming at the intersection of climate change, conflict prevention, peacebuilding, and gender equality. Objectives of the Final Evaluation 1.Assess the effectiveness of project interventions in achieving intended outcomes and contributing to immediate impacts at community, institutional, and policy levels. 2. Evaluate the coherence of project interventions with existing policies, institutions, and complementary initiatives operating at local, national, and regional levels. 3. Assess the sustainability of capacities, institutions, partnerships, and outcomes supported by the project. 4. Generate lessons learned , good practices, and provide actionable recommendations for future gender-responsive, climate-security and peacebuilding programming. Intended Users and Use of the Evaluation The primary users of the evaluation findings will be the Austrian Development Agency (ADA), International Alert, the Turkana Pastoralists Development Organization (TUPADO), and the Ethiopian Institute of Peace (EIP). The evaluation findings will be used to assess project performance, support accountability requirements, strengthen organizational learning, and inform future programming on climate change, conflict prevention, peacebuilding, and gender equality. Secondary users of the evaluation findings will include county and regional government authorities in Kenya and Ethiopia, relevant national government institutions, IGAD and other regional actors, community peace and natural resource governance structures, climate adaptation actors, civil society organizations, development partners, and practitioners working on climate security, peacebuilding, governance, and gender equality. The findings will provide evidence and lessons learned to support policy dialogue, programme design, and future interventions in the Turkana-Omo borderlands and similar contexts. Scope of the Evaluation The evaluation will cover all project components and the entire project implementation period from August 2024 to end of data collection. The evaluation will be undertaken remotely and in Kenya and Ethiopia, covering selected project intervention sites within the Turkana-Dassanech and Nyangatom-Turkana corridors. The site selection criteria should be guided by the need to ensure balanced representation across the project intervention locations. The sample should include sites from both Kenya and Ethiopia; reflect a range of project interventions and strategic result areas; capture the perspectives of diverse stakeholder groups, including women, youth, community structures, government institutions and CSO partners; and consider contextual factors such as security, accessibility, logistical feasibility. The proposed site selection should be justified in the evaluator’s inception report. The evaluation shall assess progress towards the project’s intended outcome and all outputs and examine the continued validity of the project’s Theory of Change and underlying assumptions. It will assess the project’s contribution to observed changes in institutions, relationships, capacities and practices related to climate-sensitive peacebuilding, natural resource governance and gender inclusion. Particular attention will be paid to the integration of gender equality and social inclusion, climate adaptation, conflict sensitivity, governance strengthening and cross-border cooperation across all intervention areas. The evaluation will assess the project against the OECD-DAC criteria of effectiveness, coherence and sustainability . It will also examine intended and unintended outcomes, identify factors that facilitated or hindered achievement of outcomes, and document lessons learned and good practices to inform future programming. The evaluation must apply and meet standards outlined in: ADA Guidelines for Programme and Project Evaluations International Alert conflict sensitive and gender sensitive data collection guidelines (pgs. 31-32) Key Evaluation Questions For all of the following questions, the evaluation should explicitly consider facilitating and hindering factors, and differentiate its analysis for gender, age group and vulnerability. Effectiveness 1. To what extent, and how, did the project achieve its intended outputs and outcome, particularly in empowering women and youth to meaningfully participate in cross-border conflict management and in strengthening gender-inclusive local institutions to manage transboundary climate-related conflict? 2. To what extent, and how, have policymakers at local, national, and regional levels integrated learnings from the project on the conflict–gender–climate nexus into their policies, programmes, and cross-border coordination mechanisms? 3. What unintended changes occurred among women, youth, community structures and government actors and other stakeholders as a result of the intervention? 4. Which strategies and approaches were most effective in generating positive outcomes? Coherence 5. How was the project aligned with relevant policies, strategies, and interventions related to peacebuilding (such as the Women, Peace and Security agenda), climate adaptation, natural resource management, and gender equality and women’s empowerment at local, national, and regional levels? 6. How did the project complement, coordinate with and add value to the work of governments, civil society organisations, local women’s organisations, development partners, and regional institutions operating in the target areas, and how were its different components mutually reinforcing in contributing to outcomes? 7. How effective were the coordination, collaboration and partnership arrangements among International Alert, TUPADO, EIP, government institutions, community structures, and other stakeholders, such as local women’s organisations, in supporting the achievement of project outcomes? Sustainability 8. How are the capacities, ownership, and commitments among local institutions, governance structures, and community mechanisms to continue supporting climate-sensitive and gender-responsive peacebuilding initiatives likely to be sustained beyond the project period? 9. Which project approaches, structures or practices show the greatest potential for continuation, replication or scale-up, and why? 10. What financial, institutional, political, and socio-cultural factors are likely to support or undermine the sustainability of the project’s outputs and outcomes? 11. To what extent have religious leaders, elders and other traditional or community leaders developed sustained ownership of and commitment to gender equality and women’s meaningful participation, and demonstrated leadership in promoting these principles within community peacebuilding, natural resource governance and climate adaptation measures? What evidence is there that this commitment and leadership are likely to continue beyond project support? Design and Approach / Evaluation Methodology The evaluation shall be conducted in a gender-responsive, conflict-sensitive, and participatory manner and shall adhere to the principles of Do No Harm, human rights-based approaches, standards of inclusion, informed consent, and confidentiality. The evaluators shall ensure that all data collection and engagement processes respect the dignity, rights, safety, and privacy of participants, particularly women, youth, and other potentially vulnerable groups. Throughout the evaluation process, appropriate measures shall be taken to minimize risks to participants and to ensure that the evaluation does not inadvertently exacerbate existing tensions, inequalities, or vulnerabilities. Required Data Collection Methods • Document review of relevant project documents, including proposal, 3 annual progress reports, monitoring data (indicator performance tracking table – IPTT and outcome harvesting logbook), 1 baseline survey report, 2 learning papers, 1 policy brief, impact stories videos, context data and publicly available analyses on Turkana-Omo borderlands. • Key Informant Interviews (KIIs) with project staff, implementing partners, and other relevant stakeholders • Focus Group Discussions (FGDs) and interviews with project participants and community members. Additional participatory methods such as Most Significant Change (MSC), Outcome Harvesting may be used. An Evaluation Matrix shall be developed during the inception phase, including clear indicators for each evaluation question. A Results Assessment Form (RAF) (See Annex 9 in the ADA Guidelines for Programme and Project Evaluations) shall also be completed and submitted together with the final evaluation report. The evaluation must comply with the ADA Guidelines for Programme and Project Evaluations and the OECD/DAC evaluation criteria. ADA’s cross-cutting issues (environment and climate change, and gender equality) shall be fully integrated into the evaluation design and methodology. All evaluators must have a significant contribution in all phases of the assignment and be enrolled directly in data collection, analysis and report writing. Process and Evaluation Phases The evaluation consists of three phases: Inception Phase This phase shall begin with a briefing meeting (kick-off meeting) between the evaluators, International Alert, local implementing partners, and ADA. During this phase, the evaluators shall: • Review all relevant project documentation • Analyse the intervention logic and theory of change • Conduct preliminary interviews with selected key stakeholders • Refine the methodology and sampling approach • Define the exact locations and project participants for data collection • Prepare the Evaluation Matrix and data collection tools • Submit the Inception report The Inception report shall clearly describe the evaluation design, methodology, workplan, and approach to answering each evaluation question. It must follow the structure and content outlined in Annex 5 “Quality Checklist for Inception Report” in the ADA Guidelines for Programme and Project Evaluations. The methodology will be finalised only after written approval of the Inception report by International Alert and ADA. Inquiry Phase Following approval of the Inception Report by International Alert and ADA, the evaluators shall undertake field visits to project locations in Kibish and Todonyang (Turkana) and Nyangatom and Dassanech woredas (Ethiopia) to undertake data collection with project participants. Security situation permitting, at least 2 locations on either side of the border shall be visited. If the security situation or other factors do not allow field visits, an alternative data collection approach must be agreed upon, such as remote interviews via phone or online. Key informant interviews shall be undertaken with relevant state and non-state actors in Lodwar, Turkana County and Nairobi in Kenya, and South Omo zone and Addis Ababa in Ethiopia. Following the data collection, the evaluator shall present preliminary findings and discuss potential data gaps with International Alert and ADA. Synthesis Phase This phase includes: • final data analysis and triangulation • drafting the evaluation report • formulation of findings, conclusions, and recommendations • submission of the Results Assessment Form (RAF) The findings must be clearly linked to evidence from the inception and inquiry phases and evaluation questions. Conclusions and recommendations must be practical, clearly formulated, and logically derived from the findings. The final report must follow the structure and content outlined in the Quality Checklist for evaluation reports in the ADA Guidelines for Programme and Project Evaluations (Annex 6 of the Guidelines). The synthesis phase concludes with International Alert’s and ADA’s written approval of the final evaluation report. Please note that the above are just some of the requirements for this consultancy. Particularly committed to the fight against diseases linked to unsafe water, the leading cause of death in the world, SI's interventions provide expertise in the field of access to drinking water, sanitation and hygiene promotion, but also in the essential area of food security and livelihoods. Mission Solidarités International (SI) was registered in Ethiopia in December 2022, having previously implemented a WASH in Health intervention in Jijiga, Somali Region, in 2017. In November 2023, SI became the first humanitarian actor to operate in Mao Komo Special woreda (Benishangul-Gumuz) by rehabilitating water points in areas that had been inaccessible for three years. Currently, SI is operational in two regions of the country (In Tigray Region and Amhara Region). In Tigray, bordering Eritrea, focusing on hard-to-reach areas in partnership with Mums for Mums (MfM) SI is implementing an emergency multisectoral humanitarian programme in Ahsea, Chila and Rama Woredas of central zone, to support communities affected by drought, conflict, and displacement. Running from September 2024 to December 2025 (which is now to be extended until end of June 2027), the project aims to improve access to safe water, health services, and nutrition support, while addressing gender-based violence and mental health needs. Key activities include rehabilitating water systems and health facilities, community-based malnutrition screening, cash assistance for vulnerable households, and capacity-building for local actors. SI is also working in Amhara specifically in East Gojjam and North Wolo where delivering the ECHO and CDCS projects. description:
About One Acre Fund

Founded in 2006, One Acre Fund equips 5.5 million smallholder farmers to make their farms more productive. Across nine countries that together are home to two-thirds of Africas farmers, we provide high-quality farm supplies, tree seedlings, accessible credit, modern agronomic training, and a wide range of other agricultural services. On average, this model enables any farmer to increase their income and assets on supported land by more than 35 percent, while permanently improving their resilience. This is all made possible by our team of 9,000+ full-time staff, drawn from diverse backgrounds and professions.

To learn more, please see our Why Work Here blog post.

One Acre Fund has been working with farmers in the Amhara region of Ethiopia since 2014, with a specific focus on trees since 2018. The Ethiopia program has now expanded into the South Region of Ethiopia in 2024. Our aim with the tree program is to provide not only short-term income opportunities but also long-term benefits, such as soil health improvements and erosion control, so that farmers build resilience over time.

About the Role

The Innovations & Growth Lead will be an essential part of our leadership team in one of One Acre Funds fastest-growing country programs and report directly to the Country Director. 

As an Innovations & Growth Lead, you will sit at the intersection of high-level strategy and "last-mile" delivery, shaping the strategy to plant 100 million trees and generate over $100M additional impact for 440,000 Ethiopian farmers by 2030. You will also pioneer the revenue models that will make our impact self-sustaining.

You will lead a high-performing team of innovators and M&E specialists to turn a 5-year vision into a rigorous Learning Agenda”: designing the field trials, mastering the data, and proving what works before we scale it to 440,000 households. You will ensure that every piece of data collected in the field informs our highest-level strategic decisions. If you are obsessed with evidence-based growth and love solving complex operational puzzles in the field, this is for you!.

Success is measured by your ability to reach OAF Ethiopia’s 2030 objectives. You will:

  • Support our network of 1,000+ nursery managers by improving their production and finding new ways to generate income.
  • Engineer innovative, scalable solutions to maximize income for every farmer reached, unlocking opportunities for youth and women.
  • Secure our seed supply through large-scale adoption of the best varieties and partnerships like the Jimma Research Centre.
  • Define the next frontier and move beyond existing programs to identify "whats next." You will lead the feasibility studies to transition OAF Ethiopia from a traditional NGO model to a revenue-generating organization. You will investigate the regulatory landscape and operational requirements, and research and test the most impactful agricultural practices, products, and services for our farmers.

In a single week, you could present our Learning Agenda to our Steerco, deciding which new programs (like carbon credits or market access) are ready for a pilot and which arent yet viable. You would then work with the Tree innovation team to turn raw avocado trial data into a "Go/No-Go" recommendation for national expansion, before travelling to a remote nursery to troubleshoot a pilot in person, interviewing nursery managers to identify why avocado grafting success rates are lagging, and pivoting the training approach on the spot.

Responsibilities

  • Translate our strategy into action: Lead multi-year impact strategies and translate them into specific field interventions across the organization.
  • Drive the "Learning Agenda": Define annual critical questions. You will decide which new services or products enter our pipeline based on scale and ROI, then set SMART objectives. For example, explore the possibility of adding high-value trees.
  • End-to-End Trial Management:  Design multi-year impact models, oversee the full lifecycle of field trials, empower and coach the impact team to research and implement impactful activities, from hypothesis and budgeting to operational workflows and staff training to translating it into actionable recommendations.
  • Evidence-Based Decision Making: Partner with our Monitoring & Evaluation teams to analyze trial data and drive "Go/No-Go" recommendations for the Country Director. 
  • Champion the professional evolution of your direct reports, providing the coaching and clarity needed to turn high-level organizational vision into rigorous, field-level results.

Career Growth and Development

We have a strong culture of constant learning, and we invest in developing our people. You’ll have weekly check-ins with your manager, access to mentorship and training programs, and regular feedback on your performance. We hold career reviews every six months and set aside time to discuss your aspirations and career goals. You’ll have the opportunity to shape a growing organization and build a rewarding long-term career.

Qualifications

Across all roles, these are the general qualifications we look for. For this role specifically, you will have:

  • A proven track record with a minimum of 7 years of experience in managing complex projects or operations, or social enterprise programs in emerging markets, e.g., in agricultural innovation, extension, research & development, marketing, product development, consulting or MEL in agriculture, public health, or education (including 3+ years in one of our countries of operation).
  • Experience identifying strategic gaps and designing "Learning Agendas" - knowing exactly which questions we need to answer through field trials before committing to a national-scale rollout.
  • Field-First Mindset: Significant experience living and working in rural or "last-mile" settings, with a deep understanding of the associated operational challenges.
  • Experimental Design & "Piloting" Mindset: Proven ability to design and execute field trials or pilot programs. You understand how to set up a "test vs. control" environment to see if a new intervention actually drives impact, you understand KPIs and success metrics and you have the judgment to adjust as needed when challenges come.
  • Evaluation Frameworks: Analyze qualitative/quantitative field data, and turn raw results into a "Go/No-Go" recommendation for leadership. A plus if experience working with Monitoring & Evaluation (M&E) teams to design surveys.
  • Experience managing large teams (5-10+ team members) and delivering projects successfully.
  • English required, Amharic preferred. 

Preferred Start Date

As soon as possible

Job Location

On-site in Addis Ababa or Bahir Dar, Ethiopia, with regular visits to our field areas of operations (around 35% of the time).

Benefits

Health insurance, housing, and comprehensive benefits

Eligibility

One Acre Fund can support a work permit for this role. However, nationals of (or those with an extensive professional background and work history in) our countries of operation are preferred.

 

Please note that we hire on a rolling basis which means that applications are reviewed and processed on a continuous basis until a hire is made.

One Acre Fund never asks candidates to pay any money or pay for tests at any stage of the interview process. Official One Acre Fund emails will always arrive from an @oneacrefund.org address. Please report any suspicious communication here (globalhotline@oneacrefund.org), but do not send applications or application materials to this email address.
